messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rohan is a 36-year-old South Asian man, currently employed as an accountant at a mid-sized firm in the Chicago suburbs, who presented for psychological assessment following a period of escalating distress that had begun to affect his professional functioning and what remained of his social life after a divorce finalised two years prior. His PCL-5 score of 69 places him in the severe range, and the picture that emerged across the intake and early sessions was one of a man whose childhood had never fully receded — one whose past had, in a very real sense, been living alongside him in the present.

Rohan grew up in a household defined by his father's violence toward his mother. He describes years of watching his father corner his mother in the kitchen — the specific crack of a hand against a cabinet door before the hitting began, the sound of his mother's muffled crying through a wall he pressed himself against as a small boy, the smell of the cooking she had been doing moments before the atmosphere shifted. He learned early to read the air of a room for danger, and that learning never left him. What he could never fully do, even now, was translate those years into a coherent story. The memories did not come to him as narrative. They arrived as sensation — a tightening in the chest, a flash of image without context, a feeling of dread whose origin he could not always locate. He had come to understand that he simply could not put what he witnessed into words in any way that felt adequate or complete, and this inability itself frightened him, as though the experience was too large for language to contain.

The triggers that ambushed him were specific and potent in ways that made sense given what he had witnessed. At the accounting firm, where open-plan seating meant he frequently overheard colleagues' phone calls, a raised voice — even one expressing ordinary frustration — could instantly collapse the distance between the present office and that childhood kitchen. Without warning, the full weight of the memory returned: not as a recollection but as a reliving, carrying with it the same terror he had felt as a child. His body responded as though the danger were immediate — muscles bracing, heart rate surging, breath shortening — a physical reactivity that left him visibly shaken at his desk and struggling to return to the spreadsheets in front of him. He had begun arriving earlier than his colleagues and leaving later, structuring his hours to minimise the time he spent in shared spaces, and his manager had noticed the withdrawal without understanding its cause.

The appraisals Rohan carried about what had happened — and about what it meant for his life now — were doing significant work in maintaining his distress. He was certain, with a bitterness that had calcified over decades, that his father had never faced any real consequence for what he had done. His parents remained in contact; his father was spoken of in the extended family with a kind of careful neutrality that Rohan experienced as erasure. This sense that accountability had been permanently withheld fed directly into a broader conviction that he was helpless to prevent bad things from happening to him — that harm arrived and the world simply absorbed it, indifferent. That belief kept his threat system perpetually primed: if bad things could not be stopped, then danger was always near, and his body remained in a state of constant tension, superalert to any signal that might confirm what he already feared. And when his body was already braced for threat, the memories came more easily — a raised voice, a slammed door, and the past was present again, vivid and terrorising, which in turn deepened his conviction that he was trapped in a life shaped by damage he had not caused and could not escape.

The divorce had stripped away the last structure that had organised his days around something other than vigilance. He described himself, quietly and without drama, as someone who used to be happy — a statement he offered as simple fact. What finally brought him to seek help was a morning when he sat in his car in the firm's parking garage for forty minutes, unable to go inside, aware that he could not continue managing this alone, and not yet knowing what he was hoping for, only that something had to change.
